To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

fixed-interval behavior is characterized by high rates and no post reinforcement pauses when the concurrent schedule of reinforcement is differential-reinforcement-of low rates, but by low rates and post reinforcement pauses when it is fixed ratio.
fixed-interval behavior was affected by concurrent contingencies in a manner consistent with the matching law.

the effects of differential reinforcement of low response rate on fixed-interval performance depend upon concurrent schedules of reinforcement, and that the effects of fixed ratio on fixed-interval response rates depend upon concurrent schedules as well.
In summary, our research is concerned with
human fixed-interval (FI) performance.
the effect of alternative contingencies of reinforcement on human behavior.
the effects of concurrent schedules of reinforcement upon human fixed-interval behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effect of a concurrent schedule on fixed-interval performance depends on the type of the concurrent schedule and on the prior conditioning history of the subject.
the effects of conditioning histories are mediated through their effect on the concurrent schedules of reinforcement that the subject experiences.
human fixed-interval behavior is a function of the concurrent schedule of reinforcement.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
fixed-interval responding is characterized by low constant rates when it is followed by a low rate procedure, and by high constant rates when it follows a high rate procedure.
fixed-interval schedules are more sensitive to concurrent contingencies than other schedules.
human fixed-interval behavior is determined by the interaction between conditioning history and concurrent contingencies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of conditioning histories are not always the same as those of concurrent schedules.
the effects of concurrent schedules on fixed-interval performance are more complex than the effects of conditioning-history alone.
the effects of conditioning histories upon subsequent fixed-intervals performance can be altered by the concurrent schedules.
